title: SAGE: A Unified Framework for Generalizable Object State Recognition with S

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims 'SAGE achieves up to 14.6% relative precision gain on novel state recognition' but Table 2(a) shows the highest relative gain is from 0.43 to 0.49 on ChangeIt Novel Obj State Pre@1, which is (0.49-0.43)/0.43 = 13.95%, not 14.6%. Table 2(b) shows (0.45-0.27)/0.27 = 66.7% relative gain for Novel Obj & Act, which is much higher than 14.6%. The 14.6% figure does not match any calculation from the reported results.

The abstract states SAGE 'reducing inference time compared to specialized models' and claims 'less than 5% of its inference time when the action is not provided'. Table 3 shows VidOSC takes 612.7s with unknown actions/objects while SAGE takes 29.7s. The ratio is 29.7/612.7 = 4.85%, which rounds to 5%, not 'less than 5%'. For LFC, 29.7/7278.4 = 0.41%, which is less than 5%. The claim is ambiguous about which baseline is referenced and the 5% threshold appears to be at the boundary rather than clearly below it for VidOSC.

Section 4.1 states 'we use the same pre-trained VLM, CLIP ViT-L-14 (Radford et al., 2021), which is fine-tuned with the pseudo labels and videos from HowToChange, as the vision backbone and pseudo-label generator for both the baselines and our method.' However, Table 1 shows results for CLIP, VideoCLIP, and InternVideo as separate baselines. If all methods use CLIP ViT-L-14 as stated, then VideoCLIP and InternVideo rows should not appear in Table 1 with different results, creating a contradiction about which vision encoder is actually used.

The paper states 'we compute the action embeddings as the difference between the embeddings of its end and initial object states' but does not explain how this handles the transitioning state. The framework claims to predict initial, transitioning, and end states, but the action embedding only uses initial and end states. This creates an inconsistency in how the transitioning state relates to the action representation in the embedding space.

Table 1 caption states 'variance is observed across multiple runs with standard deviations up to 3%' but no standard deviations are shown in the table, and the experimental setup in Section 4.1 does not mention multiple runs or report any variance statistics. This claim about variance cannot be verified from the presented data.

Section 4.1 states all methods use 'the same pre-trained VLM, CLIP ViT-L-14' for fair comparison, but Section 4.5 and Table 7 compare SAGE with VideoCLIP against 'reported results' from baselines that used VideoCLIP. This creates two different experimental setups (CLIP-based in main results, VideoCLIP-based in Section 4.5) that are presented as if they are comparable, when the baselines were re-implemented with different encoders in the main experiments.

Table A9 reports p-values like '1.0e-20' and '6.1e-20' which are computationally suspicious. P-values this small (effectively zero in floating-point arithmetic) suggest either an extremely large sample size or potential numerical issues. The table does not report sample sizes, effect sizes, or test statistics, making it impossible to verify if these p-values are plausible. Additionally, some comparisons show p=1.0 (e.g., 'SAGE vs. VidOSC' for Trans. Pre@1 seen), which is unusual and suggests potential issues with the statistical testing procedure.
